title: Jean Dawson Collection
services: Art direction, Apparel graphics, Poster design, Lettering
deliverables: Two tee graphics, four posters, collection graphics
lede: A self-initiated collection built around one artist’s visual world - garment graphics, posters and cut-up illustration running on a single printing language.
body: The starting question was what a run of merch would look like if it were designed the way a record sleeve is designed, rather than as a licensing exercise. Everything in the collection is built from the same kit: halftone and risograph texture, cut-up photography, and lettering drawn by hand instead of set.

Two garments anchor it. A washed green tee carries a drawn football helmet, its facemask broken into a spectrum; a washed black tee carries a photo collage under graffiti-weight lettering. Both graphics are built for the wash - heavy texture and open mid-tones, so the print reads worn rather than new on the first day.

The posters run on tight palettes: one green, one orange, one single-colour collage, and a four-colour sheet that pulls the whole series together. Held to a few inks each, they hang as a set on a wall while every sheet still stands on its own.
A self-initiated, conceptual project. Ace Studios is not affiliated with, or commissioned by, Jean Dawson - these designs are a personal exploration, made as a study of the artist’s work.
quote: Designed the way a record sleeve is designed, not as a licensing exercise.

title: Lacuna
services: Apparel graphics, Lettering, Art direction, Campaign
deliverables: Hoodie and tee graphics, wordmark, lookbook, storefront banner
lede: A streetwear line built on one hand-drawn wordmark, stretched across hoodies, tees and a lookbook.
body: The wordmark is drawn rather than set - a fast, marker-weight script that runs wide across a hoodie back, sits small at a tee hem, and wraps a globe on a back print without losing its hand.

The tee graphic pushes the other way: a swollen display letterform screened as an open halftone in a single green, with EMBRACE THE VOID set under it in a thin grotesk and deliberately knocked out of alignment.
Everything is drawn for garment-dyed blanks. Open halftones and mid-weight coverage settle into the wash rather than sitting on top of it, so the print reads worn from the first day.

The campaign banner runs the other way to the garment shots: the back print held small in a wide, warm frame with the space left open beside it, so the same artwork carries a storefront header without a crop fighting the type.
quote: Drawn rather than set, so it keeps its hand at any size.

title: 480 BC
deliverables: Tee and shorts graphics, brand mark
lede: An apparel capsule built around the Battle of Thermopylae, with line-drawn armour and a mark cut from the same hand.
body: The mark is a compressed, angular 480 that reads as much like a sigil as a number. It sits small on the chest, large on the leg, and holds at either size because the strokes are cut at a single angle.

The garment graphics are all line: a helmet drawn in one weight and broken so it wraps the side seam of the tee, and a pair of gorillas squared off across the front of the shorts. A second colourway drops the contrast to a tonal print on black.
A block of text about the battle is set small at the hem. It gives the capsule its name and does the explaining, so the graphics do not have to.
quote: The text at the hem does the explaining, so the graphics do not have to.

title: Music & Culture Posters
lede: A run of artist posters at two print sizes, each built from its own typographic idea rather than a house template.
body: The set is deliberately not a system. One sheet is blown out to pure black and white with the grain left in, one runs a chrome display face across a split field, one interleaves the figure between stacked letterforms so the type sits both behind and in front.

Each poster carries its own information layer - tour dates set vertically down the edge, a discography line across the foot, a block of body copy justified under the title. The type does the work a caption would otherwise have to do.
Printed at 18x24 and 20x30, with the scale set from the largest viewing distance down: the name reads across a room, the small copy only pays off up close.
Self-initiated. These are personal poster studies of artists I listen to. They were not commissioned, and they are not affiliated with or endorsed by the artists.
quote: Format and intent hold them together, not a shared grid.

title: Screen Posters
lede: Alternative posters for four titles, all built on one two-colour system.
body: Where the music posters are deliberately unalike, these run to a single set of rules: two inks, a coarse halftone, a panel grid, and a synopsis justified across the foot.

Holding every title to the same structure moves the work into the edit - which frames get chosen, how the panels are weighted against each other, and where the title block is allowed to break the grid it sits in.
The halftone is set coarse on purpose. At poster size the dot is visible from a normal viewing distance, which keeps the source footage reading as print rather than as a screenshot.
Self-initiated. Unofficial poster studies made as personal work. They are not affiliated with, licensed by, or endorsed by the rights holders of the titles shown.
quote: Two inks and one grid, so the differences land in the edit.

title: Team & Club Apparel
deliverables: Tees for three organisations, badge marks
lede: Shirts for a college honours programme, a wildlife society and a high school volleyball season.
body: Team merch has a harder brief than it looks. It has to name the organisation, the event and the year, survive one screen-print colour, and still be something a person will wear when the season is over.

Each mark is built as a badge that works standing alone: an oval lockup for the volleyball season, a halftone crest for the golf classic, and a stacked monogram for the wildlife society that opens up into a full illustration on the back.
All three are drawn for a single screen on a garment-dyed blank, which keeps a run affordable for a club paying out of its own budget.
quote: It has to survive one screen-print colour and still be worn after the season.

title: Simply Alone Studios
lede: A hoodie capsule built on one quiet wordmark, held small enough to read as a label rather than a slogan.
body: The graphic is held deliberately small. A stacked wordmark with a rule under it, sized and placed so it reads as a garment label rather than something shouting across a room.

The lockup does its work with weight rather than scale: a heavy sans for the name, a lighter cut for the sub-line, and a year set in script running through both. Three weights in a graphic barely six inches wide, which is what keeps it legible without getting louder.
A second piece runs looser - layered type and a drawn ellipse over a washed brown body, printed soft so it reads as something already worn in rather than new.
quote: Held small enough to read as a label, not a slogan.

title: Rhinestone Cowboy
lede: One red ink, a drawn rider, and a wordmark that splits serif against script.
body: The lockup sets a spurred serif over a looping script, so the two halves of the name pull against each other the way the phrase does.
The rider is drawn as an open line illustration and printed in the same single red, which lets it run large across the front and then wrap small around the hip on the back without a second screen.
Held to one ink on white throughout, so the whole capsule prints in a single pass.
quote: One ink, one pass, and the drawing still carries it.

title: Album Art
lede: Covers built to survive being shrunk to a thumbnail without losing what they are.
body: A cover now lives at two sizes that could not be further apart: a 3000px master and a postage stamp in a streaming queue. Everything here is designed at the small size first and then allowed to reward the large one.
That means one dominant shape per cover - a rose, a vortex, a single blown-out figure - with the type either cut into it or held well clear of it, never competing at thumbnail size.
Texture does the rest. Scanned grain, torn edges and heavy contrast give each sleeve a physical read that a clean digital render would not have.
quote: Designed at thumbnail size first, then allowed to reward the large one.

title: Motion
lede: Short loops built for a feed: silent, square, and legible in the first half second.
body: Everything here is cut to run under eight seconds and to work with the sound off, because that is how it will actually be seen. The first frame carries the whole idea; the motion is what makes you stop.
The studio idents are the test case - a mark that assembles and holds, short enough to sit in front of a piece of work without becoming an obstacle to it.
Exported silent and compressed hard. A loop that takes three seconds to load has already lost the person it was made for.
quote: The first frame carries the idea. The motion is what makes you stop.

title: Type Studies
lede: Two sheets made to work a problem out rather than to sell anything.
body: The first is a grid stress test: a single column of statements broken across weights and sizes until the hierarchy nearly collapses, then pulled back one step from the edge.
The second goes the other way - layered scans, halftone and torn paper with the type buried in it, to see how little of a word can still be read once the texture is fighting it.
Neither was briefed. They exist to find the limit, which is what makes them useful on the jobs that are briefed.
quote: They exist to find the limit, which is what makes them useful on the jobs that are briefed.
